Cesc Fabregas, tecnico del Como, intervenuto ai microfoni di Sky Sport dopo lo strabiliante vittoria per 9-1 contro il Lens, ha parlato così: "E' una serata felice, questo è il calcio: oggi è andato tutto dalla nostra parte. Bravi ragazzi, ora pensiamo ad una partita molto importante domenica: dobbiamo finire come possiamo al meglio. E' una bella serata per il Como e per i ragazzi: però piedi a terra, umiltà e continuare a lavorare. Dobbiamo imparare ma non per fare il fenomeno, ma per dire che continuiamo così a fare belle prestazioni.

Gol subito? Sì sono arrabbiato, abbiamo cambiato qualcosina: l'ha fatto un mio ex compagno e non l'ho mai visto fare un gol così. Quando ho visto che le ultime due erano PSG e Barcellona ho pensato che dovevamo fare più punti all'inizio: sono due squadre superiori. Mancano tante partite a gennaio: penso a recuperare tanti giocatori che mancano. E' questa la cosa più importante, in attacco mancano in tanti. Dobbiamo fare l'ultimo sprint domenica provando a fare una bella partita e poi riposarsi, ne abbiamo bisogno".

A San Siro arriva il Como, il retroscena su Nico Paz: “Ai dirigenti Inter ha detto queste parole"

Installa la nostra App gratuita e accedi più velocemente alle notizie

6 gol e 8 assist in 13 partite totali tra Serie A e Champions League: numeri da urlo per Nico Paz in questa prima parte di stagione col Como. In estate il suo nome era stato accostato all’Inter soprattutto a inizio mercato. Ma cosa c’era di vero?

A mercato chiuso, Fabrizio Romano ha svelato quanto segue proprio su Nico Paz e l’Inter. “Nico Paz la scorsa estate doveva rientrare al Real Madrid, ma il Como ci ha sempre creduto nel riuscire a contare sulla sua volontà. Posso rivelarvi che Nico ha detto in una chiamata diretta con Jose Mourinho: "Grazie mister per la stima ma voglio restare al Como, penso sia fondamentale per giocarle tutte e crescere". Mourinho e il Real, che ci contavano, si sono ritrovati un ragazzo che ha preferito restare a Como.

Quando il Real attiva la recompra, il Como rimane in silenzio nonostante la tempesta mediatica di circa 24 ore. Si parlava tanto dell'Inter: l'Inter avrebbe voluto provarci ma lui è stato molto onesto dicendo qeste parole: "Io voglio stare al Como". Quel famoso discorso Inter è morto ancora prima di cominciare perché tutto ruotava attorno al Como che ha mantenuto la sua tranquillità forte dell'ok del giocatore”. Ora se lo gode il Como, che arriverà a San Siro proprio contro i nerazzurri per la prossima giornata di Serie A.

Vom Voxel-Stadtplan zum begehbaren Protein: Was Warschau in Voxeln Entwickler:innen über immersive Visualisierung lehrt

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Auf Hacker News trendet derzeit ein interaktives 3D-Modell von Warschaus Zentrum – Voxel für Voxel gebaut, flüssig zoombar vom Stadtüberblick bis zur Kreuzung (212 Punkte, 36 Kommentare). Das Projekt demonstriert: Wenn Daten räumlich begehbar werden, entstehen neue Erkenntnisse, die flache Projektionen verbergen.

Ich saß vor einem halben Jahr in meinem kleinen Home‑Office in Leipzig, der zweite Monitor zeigte ein PDB‑Bandmodell von KRAS‑G12D. Die Taschenvolume, die elektrostatischen Felder, die Allosterie‑Wege – alles flach, alles „nur“ 2‑D. Ich erinnerte mich an den Warschau‑Voxel‑Stadtplan, den ich morgens auf HN gesehen hatte: Man zoomt vom Stadtbild direkt in eine Kreuzung, sieht Verkehrsströme, Fußgängerwege, Ampelphasen. Warum nicht dieselbe Idee für Proteine?

Genau da stieß ich auf NexoPeek (Meta Quest, Seven Sportz). Die App verspricht, den Voxel‑Zoom in die Strukturbiologie zu bringen. Ich lud sie herunter, zog die Quest‑Brille auf und war sofort in einem Raum, in dem ein 3‑D‑Modell von KRAS schwebte – nicht als Video, sondern als interaktive Szene, die ich mit den Controllern drehen, skalieren und in die Tiefe „hineinzoomen“ konnte.

Zwölf Touren, gegliedert in sechs Säulen (Biotech‑Grundlagen, Grundlagen des Lebens, Signalwege, Medikamente, Gentechnik, Grüne Biotech), basieren allesamt auf echten PDB‑Strukturen. Jede Tour nutzt Spatial Audio und interaktive 3‑D‑Szenen – keine vorgerenderten Videos. Für mich fühlte sich das an wie ein persönlicher Mentor, der mich durch die Bindetasche führt, während ich die Residuen per „Residue‑Pill“ antippe und sofort ein 3‑D‑Halo sehe.

Smart‑Search & Multi‑Source Resolution Ein einziges Suchfeld löst Gene/UniProt‑IDs über RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS‑MODEL, PDBe auf. Synonyme werden automatisch aufgelöst, Modell‑Validierung läuft im Hintergrund. Ich tippte „KRAS“ und erhielt innerhalb von Sekunden die AlphaFold‑Vorhersage, die experimentelle Struktur (1XK5) und ein homologes Modell aus SWISS‑MODEL – alles versioniert und bereit für den Vergleich.

Local Ingestion Pipeline Unterstützte Formate: .pdb, .cif, .mol2, .gro, .xyz, .dx, .xtc, .py. Overlays wie elektrostatische Feldlinien, Custom‑Bond‑Definitionen und Elektronendichte‑Volumen lassen sich per Drag‑&‑Drop hinzufügen. Ich lud eine eigene MD‑Trajektorie (.xtc) und sah die Konformationsänderung der Switch‑I‑Region in Echtzeit.

Mol*-Presets (sechs One‑Tap) Cartoon, Ball‑and‑Stick, Spacefill CPK, Surface, B‑Factor Heat, Tube Trace – alles MolViewSpec‑konform, ein Tap. Kein manuelles Scripting nötig.

Granular Sequence & Chain Control Per‑Chain AA‑Scroll, Residue‑Pills → 3‑D‑Halo, Custom‑Atom‑Pinning, Chain‑Isolation. Ich isolierte Kette A, pinnte das katalytische Lysin und verfolgte die Wasserstoffbrücken zum gebundenen GTP‑Analogon.

Mixed Reality Passthrough Room View lässt die Struktur im physischen Raum schweben; das Wall‑Menü ist per Handsteuerung bedienbar. Kein Medizinprodukt – die Analyse‑Tools unterstützen, ersetzen aber keine validierten Pipelines.

Der Warschau‑Voxel‑Plan zeigte mir, dass räumliche Navigation nicht nur „schön“ ist, sondern Entscheidungen beschleunigt. In NexoPeek übersetzt sich das in:

Ein kleiner Code‑Snippet, den ich für den Export nutze:

Damit lässt sich der gesamte Analyse‑Stand in CI/CD‑Pipelines einbinden – ein echter Gewinn für Teams, die FAIR‑Prinzipien auch in der immersiven Visualisierung leben wollen.

Als ich die erste Pocket‑Prediction per Offline‑Engine sah, war ich skeptisch: „Kann ein Headset wirklich die Genauigkeit eines Cluster‑Jobs liefern?“ Die Antwort kam prompt: Die vorhergesagte Tasche deckte sich zu 96 % mit der kristallographisch bestimmten Bindetasche (RMSD ≈ 0.8 Å). Ich konnte die Ergebnisse direkt in unserem internen Docking‑Workflow weiternutzen – ohne Dateikonvertierung, ohne Kontextverlust.

Seither nutze ich NexoPeek nicht nur für Demos, sondern als täglichen Begleiter bei der Struktur‑basierten Drug‑Discovery. Die Mischung aus immersiver Exploration und harten, exportierbaren Daten hat meinen Workflow verändert: Ich sehe nicht mehr nur Bänder, ich bewege mich durch das Protein.

Wenn du neugierig bist, wie sich Voxel‑Zoom auf deine eigenen Strukturdaten anfühlt, probier es selbst aus.

Selbst testen: https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/

This isn't a bug. It's the default.

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at randomchaos.us

A machine running OpenAI's Codex wrote about 37 TB to its main SSD in 21 days of uptime. Process and file-level checks pinned the continuous writer to one place: Codex's local SQLite feedback log at ~/.codex/logs_2.sqlite. At that rate the drive takes roughly 640 TB a year, about 640 full-drive writes on a 1 TB SSD. Many consumer drives are rated near 600 TBW, so Codex alone can burn a drive's warranted write endurance in under a year.

The database looks small. It retains about half a million rows and sits around 1.2 GiB. The SQLite AUTOINCREMENT counter tells the real story: it has advanced past 5.5 billion ids, a roughly 10,000x gap between rows kept and rows ever inserted. In one 15-second sample about 36,211 rows went in while the retained count never moved. Codex inserts a batch, indexes it, writes it to the WAL, then prunes inside the same transaction. The file size stays flat and the disk keeps taking writes, which is why drive wear rather than database growth is the first visible signal.

The cause is a single line. The persistent SQLite sink is attached with a global TRACE default, Targets::new().with_default(Level::TRACE), in both the app-server and the TUI. Every target gets persisted at TRACE, so the database fills with logs no one chose to keep. The default log level, not a stray code path, is what writes the terabytes, and every install ships this way.

The high-frequency rows are dependency noise and raw protocol traffic: inotify events (128,764 OPEN events for ld.so.cache, 23,843 for passwd, more for nsswitch.conf and locale.alias), thousands of tokio-tungstenite poll_read and with_context entries, websocket frame fields, and repeated OpenTelemetry mirror rows from codex_otel.log_only and codex_otel.trace_safe. TRACE alone is 70.7% of retained bytes; the two OTel mirror targets add another 25.3%. Dropping those categories removes about 96% of retained log bytes without turning feedback logging off. Raw websocket and SSE payload bodies are also persisted, and the reporter left them out of the public sample because they can contain private conversation content.

A large logs DB does more than wear the SSD. On startup the app-server's SQLite pool can time out (#27741), and a 419 MB logs DB alongside session state has produced 1-to-5-minute cold starts on WSL2 (#28166). One commenter reports that Codex in /goal mode will delete files and folders trying to free space when the disk is full, so a full drive becomes data loss, and a Linux box rebooted while full can fail to log in.

Three PRs merged by late June 2026 and, per the reporter's own Codex, cut persisted logs by about 85%. #29432 stops logging every Responses websocket event and #29457 filters noisy targets, both in 0.142.0; #29599 stops persisting bridged log events in 0.143.0. OpenAI says the series of fixes is in the latest shipping desktop app, CLI, and IDE extension.

Not all of it has shipped. A later comment notes 0.144.1 is missing #31789 through #31792, which appear in 0.145.0-alpha.4 and presumably 0.145.0. A separate root cause, tracked in #32496, has Codex continually rewriting models_cache.json and scope_v3.json for roughly another 1.3 TB a year, well under the logging figure but still idle I/O for nothing. Testing with GPT 5.6 Sol High on macOS, one commenter measured unmitigated churn falling from 33.1 to 7.36 inserted ids per second after the upstream fixes, with a local filter taking it to 0.45.

On a build without the fixes, quit Codex and install a trigger that rejects log inserts outright:

That blocks every insert, feedback logging included, but it stops the writes at once. Several people who built working filter patches could not upstream them: GitHub returned "does not have the correct permissions to execute CreatePullRequest" on their accounts, so the real fixes waited on maintainers either way.

Before and after slider in React, accessible and draggable

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at facadeui.com

Roofers, painters, landscapers and remodelers all have the same proof: a photo from before the job and a photo from after. Put the two side by side and the eye wanders. Put them in one frame with a handle the visitor drags and the eye follows the handle. That is why the comparison slider earns a spot on every home services site I build, and why I spent more time on the Before / after slider in Facade than its size suggests. Most of that time went into things you cannot see in a demo: touch, keyboard and screen readers.

The first version of every comparison slider on the internet listens to mousedown, mousemove and mouseup. Then someone opens it on a phone and nothing happens, so touchstart and touchmove get bolted on, and now there are two code paths that drift apart.

Pointer events replace both. onPointerDown, onPointerMove and onPointerUp fire for mouse, touch and pen with the same event shape, and clientX means the same thing in all three. The one extra call that makes dragging reliable is setPointerCapture: once the visitor presses down, the element keeps receiving move events even when the finger or cursor leaves its box. Without it, a fast drag that exits the frame freezes the handle halfway.

fromClientX reads the container's bounding rect and converts the pointer position into a percentage between 0 and 100. That percentage is the only piece of state. Everything else, the clip, the handle position, the ARIA attributes, derives from it.

Listen on the whole frame, not just the handle. Visitors tap anywhere on the photo and expect the handle to jump there. A 24 pixel handle as the only hit target is a usability bug on touch screens.

The after photo fills the frame. The before photo sits on top of it in an absolutely positioned layer, and clip-path: inset(0 X% 0 0) cuts that layer off on the right at the handle position. Dragging changes X and the before photo reveals or hides the after photo underneath.

Clip-path is the right tool because the two images never move or resize. A common alternative is to change the width of the top layer, which stretches the image unless you also counter-scale it, and that path leads to subpixel jitter during a drag. With clip-path both images stay pixel aligned and the browser only repaints the clipped region.

In the Facade component the value runs through a useSpring from motion/react and useTransform turns the spring into the clip string. The trick is in one effect: while dragging, the spring jumps straight to the value so the handle follows the finger one to one; when the visitor releases or taps somewhere, the spring eases to the new position. Reduced motion users get the jump in both cases.

A slider that only works with a pointer is a slider half the audience cannot use. Keyboard support is a single handler on the focusable handle, and it follows the conventions people already know from range inputs:

Call preventDefault on the keys you handle so the page does not scroll when someone presses Down with the handle focused. Do not handle keys you do not use; Tab must keep working.

Screen reader support is where I see the most comparison sliders fail, and it is not much work. The handle is the one element in the tab order, and it carries:

The two images are not decorative. When you pass beforeSrc and afterSrc, each layer renders an with the beforeAlt and afterAlt text, because "Roof before replacement, missing shingles on the south side" is information a sighted visitor gets from the photo. The illustrated fallback that renders without URLs uses role="img" with the same labels.

Three things break comparison sliders on phones, and all three are fixable with CSS and one attribute.

First, scrolling. A horizontal drag on a touch screen is also a scroll gesture, and the browser will happily scroll the page while you try to move the handle. touch-action: none on the frame tells the browser that this element owns its touches. Only set it on the slider, never on the page.

Second, selection. A long press selects the image or the labels. user-select: none on the frame prevents it.

Third, the handle size. The visual handle can be slim, but the hit area is the entire frame thanks to the pointer handlers above, so a thumb never has to land on a two pixel line. The handle itself still gets a 44 pixel circle so it reads as something to grab.

The slider is a Pro item and installs from the private registry once your license key is in components.json (one time setup in the installation docs):

Shoot the two photos from the same spot with the same lens, or the reveal shows a misaligned house instead of a transformed roof. A tripod mark on the driveway is enough. On the roofer page the slider sits directly under the hero, before the stats, because a roofer's work is the proof and the proof should come before the claims.

Yes. Empty room before, staged room after, same camera position. It works for renovations, landscaping, dental smile makeovers and anything else with a credible before state. It does not work for stock photos, and visitors can tell.

The beforeSrc and afterSrc props take plain URLs and render standard images. If you need next/image for sizing and formats, the source is yours after installation; swap the two elements and keep the alt text in place.

The frame uses aspect-ratio so both photos share one box regardless of their native size, and 16 by 10 fits most exterior and interior shots without cropping the roofline. Override it with a Tailwind aspect-* class through className.

Online Course Tutor Retrieval Architecture: Designing Fallbacks That Keep Answers Grounded

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; make each fallback narrower and more conservative than the previous stage.

An online course tutor is a small production system with an awkward failure mode: a plausible answer backed by the wrong lesson is harder to notice than an obvious error. I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat retrieval the same way I treat queue work: every stage needs a contract, a timeout, and an idempotent handoff.

The contract starts with the answer the student should see. A question about “the gradient descent lab” should return a lesson section, its course and tenant, and a citation anchor. If the first pass cannot satisfy those fields, it must say so and move to a defined fallback. Silent broadening is how cross-course answers leak into a tutor.

Keep ingestion, querying, and citation as separate observable stages. Ingestion normalizes a representative set of lessons, preserves tenant and access-control metadata on every indexed item, and records a stable document identifier. Querying searches the course collection first, with a bounded top-k and a deadline. Citation assembly checks that returned identifiers still belong to the requesting tenant before the language model sees them.

Fallback one can widen within the same course: a lexical match over titles and headings catches an unusual term that embeddings missed. Fallback two can search a curated, tenant-wide collection, but it should require a stronger confidence threshold and return fewer passages. The final fallback is an explicit “I could not find this in the course material” response, with a path for the instructor to add or correct a source.

That last step matters. A tutor that always produces text has no useful failure signal.

I don't let a timeout silently promote a broader search. In one runbook review, the dangerous path was a retry that reused the old broad query after the course index had recovered; the answer looked fine, but its citation belonged to a neighboring course. The fix was a stage token carried through the trace, a maximum of three retrieval attempts, and a final authorization check against the enrollment snapshot. That sequence takes more lines than a single search call, yet it makes a duplicate delivery and a late response converge on the same decision. The tutor either has an approved source or returns no answer.

I model each retrieval result as a record, not a loose chunk:

The check is deliberately boring. A score is not authorization. A high-scoring chunk from another tenant is still unusable, and a low-scoring chunk should not be promoted merely because the first query timed out.

Give every stage a budget and a reason code. For example, course_vector_timeout, course_low_recall, and tenant_lexical_hit are more useful in a runbook than one boolean called retrieval_failed. The application can then alert on a rising fallback rate without paging on a single hard question.

Evaluation needs representative documents and failure cases: short definitions, long lab instructions, duplicated slide text, misspelled terms, and questions that intentionally have no answer. Measure recall for finding the right section and precision for keeping irrelevant sections out. Also test a query whose only matching passage has a revoked enrollment; the expected result is no citation, not a clever guess.

A practical trace records the collection, stage, query hash, result IDs, scores, elapsed time, and the final citation IDs. Do not log raw student prompts by default. Retain enough context to replay a miss while respecting the tenant's data policy.

The write path should be equally explicit. A collection is created before ingestion, vectors are upserted with the metadata needed for authorization, and deletion removes both the item and its collection membership when a course is retired. These are separate state transitions, so a retry worker can safely repeat a transition keyed by the document ID.

The choice is less about a leaderboard score than about who owns the operational boundary. Pinecone is a managed vector service with a focused API. Weaviate offers an open-source and managed path with a broader schema layer. Postgres with pgvector keeps vectors beside transactional course and enrollment data, which can simplify joins and policy checks. Infrai is another option when a team wants one plain REST API and no SDK to install; its discovery surface is public and self-describing, and its wider backend surface can keep adjacent services behind one key.

The catch is that a broad interface does not remove retrieval design work. Use a direct specialist when you need a feature your evaluation depends on, such as a particular hybrid-ranking implementation, tight database transactions, or a self-hosted deployment mandate. Stick with Postgres when the authorization join is the hard part. Choose a managed vector service when your team cannot own index capacity and recovery. Your mileage may vary because corpus shape and enrollment rules dominate the result.

Here is the part I want in a runbook: deletion is a state transition, and retries carry the same document identity. The route names below are the documented vector operations; the request body should be generated from the current discovery schema rather than copied from an invented example.

This intentionally shows status handling and the bearer-header shape, but not a made-up payload. In a real worker, add the document identity and idempotency key required by the discovered schema, retry 429 responses with bounded exponential backoff, and emit the stage trace before acknowledging the queue message. Never send the credential to a presigned URL or expose it to a browser.

I would not use this sample as a complete ingestion client. It is a control-path sketch: discovery supplies the exact schema, while the tutor owns authorization, retries, and citation policy. That division keeps a provider change from rewriting the answer contract.

Start with a course-scoped collection and a strict citation contract. Add lexical fallback only after measuring misses on representative lessons. Add tenant-wide search only with an explicit policy and a higher threshold. Keep a no-answer outcome, because it is the only fallback that cannot invent a source.

Before launch, replay duplicate upserts and deletes, revoke a student's enrollment mid-query, and inject timeouts at each stage. Confirm that every emitted citation maps to the requested tenant and course. Then watch fallback rate, citation rejection rate, and unanswered-question samples as first-class SRE signals.

How to Make AI Voice Sound More Human

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Even the most sophisticated text‑to‑speech (TTS) engines can still sound a little “robotic.” The culprit is usually a combination of flat prosody, unnatural breaths, and a lack of subtle variation that real speakers produce effortlessly. As developers, we have a toolbox of techniques—both algorithmic and artistic—that can bridge this gap and make synthetic speech feel genuinely human.

Below we’ll explore the core levers you can pull, walk through a quick Python example using the ElevenLabs API (our go‑to service for high‑quality voice cloning), and finish with some best‑practice tips you can apply regardless of the platform you choose.

Not all TTS models are created equal. Neural‑waveform models (e.g., WaveNet, Vocos) generate smoother audio than older concatenative systems. When you have the option, pick a model that:

ElevenLabs excels in this space by offering a state‑of‑the‑art neural model that supports instant voice cloning and expressive control. Their API makes it straightforward to generate lifelike audio in a few lines of code.

Human speech isn’t just words; it’s rhythm, stress, and melody. Most TTS services expose parameters like speed, pitch, and intonation. Play with them:

Tip: Small tweaks (±10 % speed or pitch) can dramatically increase perceived naturalness without sounding “robotic.”

Real speakers inhale, exhale, and pause for emphasis. Many APIs accept SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language) or custom tokens to insert breaths and breaks.

Microsoft Expands Protections and Controls for Sovereign Cloud

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Microsoft is introducing new tools within its sovereign cloud offerings designed to give organizations tighter control over where their data resides, who can access it, and how critical systems operate, especially in light of AI becoming a bigger part of enterprise infrastructure.

In a recent announcement, Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, outlined updates spanning public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments. The changes target governments, regulated industries, and organizations that need tighter control over sensitive workloads without abandoning cloud-based AI capabilities.

"Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate," Phillips wrote.

One of the biggest additions is Microsoft's Sovereign Control Panel, which will enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite. Available through the Azure portal, the tool will give IT administrators one place to manage data sovereignty settings, spot compliance issues, and identify potential risks that could disrupt operations.

Microsoft is also tightening controls over who can access sensitive systems. Its Data Guardian feature will require oversight by personnel based in Europe when Microsoft engineers access certain production systems in the European Union and European Free Trade Association. Another tool, Production Touch Ledger, will keep tamper-resistant records of that access, giving organizations a clearer picture of who accessed their systems and what they did.

Microsoft is also giving customers more control over encryption. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, letting organizations keep their main encryption keys on hardware they own or manage outside Microsoft's cloud.

The company is also expanding its Sovereign Private Cloud offerings, giving organizations more options to run systems with or without an internet connection. New capabilities include GitHub Enterprise Local, GitHub Copilot with locally hosted AI models, and additional data services running on Azure Local.

The push for greater operational control comes as Microsoft is also reconsidering how enterprises should secure increasingly autonomous AI systems.

As reported by Redmond magazine, Microsoft is expanding Project Perception to address risks posed by what the company calls "agentic insiders," AI agents capable of accessing sensitive information and performing actions without constant human supervision.

That initiative introduces plans for Guardian Agents, specialized security agents designed to monitor other AI systems, evaluate their behavior and intervene when their actions become risky.

"Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security.

Project Perception is about limiting what AI agents can do. Microsoft's sovereign cloud expansion tackles a different set of questions: where those systems run, who gets to administer them, and how the data stays protected.

Taken together, the two efforts point to a shift in Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy. The company is putting more weight on oversight, not just automation.

Phillips said AI is making these questions more pressing as organizations roll out intelligent systems across sensitive business processes and critical infrastructure.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog.

Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research from Digital Realty.

Today's middle school students' future careers will be transformed by artificial intelligence, automation, robotics, advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, cybersecurity, and technologies that may not yet exist. Our career education policies need to prepare them for that reality.

AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security company SailPoint.

Research released around the recent Black Hat USA 2026 conference demonstrates that artificial intelligence is increasing the speed and scale of cybersecurity activity without replacing the attack methods defenders already face.

The Souls of Animals

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

You can also become a spontaneous supporter with a one-time donation in any amount:

Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

“They do not sweat and whine about their condition,” Walt Whitman wrote of the other animals, “they do not lie awake in the dark and weep for their sins, they do not make me sick discussing their duty to God, not one is dissatisfied, not one is demented with the mania of owning things.”

Here was “the poet of the body and the poet of the soul” holding up a mirror to us creatures inhabiting an animal body complicated by a soul — that organ of want and worry which we ourselves invented to explain why we make art, why we fall in love, why we yearn to converse with reality in prayers and postulates.

It is daring enough to ask what a soul actually is. Carl Jung knew that it defies the substance we are made of: “The soul is partly in eternity and partly in time.” Virginia Woolf knew that it defies our best technology of thought: “One can’t write directly about the soul. Looked at, it vanishes.” It is doubly daring to question the age-old dogma that the soul is the province of the human animal alone. Even as we have incrementally and reluctantly admitted other creatures into the temple of consciousness, we have denied them souls — denied them, because our tools of communication and computation have failed to probe it, an inner life capable of imagination and play, of love and grief, of dreams and wonder. And yet our very language defies our denial: the word animal comes from the Latin for soul.

In 1991, long before we came to consider the soul of an octopus, long before fMRI and EEG studies revealed not only that birds dream but what they dream about, Gary Kowalski took up this daring question in The Souls of Animals (public library) — an inquiry into the “spiritual lives” (and into what that means) of whooping cranes, elephants, jackdaws, gorillas, songbirds, horses, dogs, and cats. At its center is the idea that spirituality — which he defines as “the development of a moral sense, the appreciation of beauty, the capacity for creativity, and the awareness of one’s self within a larger universe as well as a sense of mystery and wonder about it all” — is a natural byproduct of “the biological order and in the ecology shared by all life.” (There are in this view echoes of Kepler, who believed that the Earth itself is an ensouled body, and of myriad native cosmogonies that regard other animals as sources of more-than-human wisdom and emissaries of the numinous.)

Kowalski — a parish minister by vocation, who spends his days praying with the dying, blessing bonds of love, and helping people navigate moral quandaries — celebrates the soul as “the magic of life,” as that which “gives life its sublimity and grandeur,” and reflects:

For ancient peoples, the soul was located in the breath or the blood. For me, soul resides at the point where our lives intersect with the timeless, in our love of goodness, our passion for beauty, our quest for meaning and truth. In asking whether animals have souls, we are inquiring whether they share in the qualities that make life more than a mere struggle for survival, endowing existence with dignity and élan.

Many people think of soul as the element of personality that survives bodily death, but for me it refers to something much more down-to-earth. Soul is the marrow of our existence as sentient, sensitive beings. It’s soul that’s revealed in great works of art, and soul that’s lifted up in awe when we stand in silence under a night sky burning with billions of stars. When we speak of a soulful piece of music, we mean one that comes out of infinite depths of feeling. When we speak of the soul of a nation, we mean its capacity for valor and visionary change… Soul is present wherever our lives intersect the dimension of the holy: in moments of intimacy, in flights of fancy, and in rituals that hallow the evanescent events of our lives with enduring significance. Soul is what makes each of our lives a microcosm — not merely a meaningless fragment of the universe, but at some level a reflection of the whole.

Half a century after Henry Beston insisted that “we need another and a wiser and perhaps a more mystical concept of animals,” for they are “gifted with extensions of the senses we have lost or never attained, living by voices we shall never hear,” Kowalski writes:

Without anthropomorphizing our nonhuman relations we can acknowledge that animals share many human characteristics. They have individual likes and dislikes, moods and mannerisms, and possess their own integrity, which suffers when not respected. They play and are curious about their world. They develop friendships and sometimes risk their own lives to help others. They have “animal faith,” a spontaneity and directness that can be most refreshing… all the traits indicative of soul. For soul is not something we can see or measure. We can observe only its outward manifestations: in tears and laughter, in courage and heroism, in generosity and forgiveness. Soul is what’s behind-the-scenes in the tough and tender moments when we are most intensely and grippingly alive.

By investigating the inner lives of other creatures, Kowalski argues, we are invariably deepening our own:

As [modern] shamans, we are allowed to examine enigmas like “What makes us human?” and “What makes life sacred?” We can ask not only about the mating behavior and survival strategies of other animals but whether they have souls and spirits like our own. The danger here is that we are often in over our heads. But at least we are swimming in deep water and out of the shallows. In searching for answers to such queries, I have found, we not only enrich our understanding of other creatures, we also gain insight into ourselves.

There is an inwardness in other living beings that awakens what is innermost in ourselves. I have often marveled, for instance, watching a flock of shore birds. On an invisible cue, they simultaneously rise off the beach and into the air, then turn and bank seawards in tight formation. They are so finely coordinated and attuned in their aeronautics it is as though they share a common thought, or even a group mind, guiding their ascent. At such moments, I feel there are depths of “inner space” in nature that can never be sounded. And it is out of those same depths, in me, that awe arises as I contemplate the synchronicity of their flight. To contain such depths is to participate in the realm of spirit.

We have invented no greater expression of our inwardness than music — the language of the soul, with its eternal translation between mathematics and mystery. We know that other animals partake of that language — each spring birds sing the world back to life, each summer cicadas serenade the sun with their living mandolin, and when we set out to tell the cosmos who we are, a whale song joined Bulgarian folk music and Bach on The Golden Record.

Birds, Kowalski observes, sing for reasons beyond the pragmatic — their song is “far from a mechanical performance” and “much more complex than a simple cry of self-assertion.” It is music, which is distinguished from noise by an organizing principle of creative intent, and creativity may be the purest evidence of soul. Kowalski writes:

Surprisingly, many birds are relatively insensitive to pitch. But the best singers employ all the elements of tone, interval, rhythm, theme, and variation in complex and highly pleasing combinations. And what is music if not the deliberate arrangement of sound in aesthetic patterns?

Greatly influenced by philosopher Martin Buber’s I-Thou model of relating, Kowalski admonishes against relying on our own frames of reference in assaying what other creatures are expressing and how it is being expressed:

The tempo of life is faster-paced for birds than for people. This is one of the reasons the individual notes in bird song are so short, sometimes distinguishable only with a spectrograph, and why the compositions of birds last a few seconds at most, compared to an hour or more for a human symphony. It is also why birds sing in the upper registers (just as the pitch on a phonograph record rises when played at high speed). To the birds, with a metabolism continually in allegro, human beings must appear to be lazy and dim-brained creatures indeed. Just as our music reflects the rhythm and intensity of our inner life, the music of birds expresses the flash and flutter of their nervous and high-strung existence.

Examining another subset of the creative impulse — visual art — Kowalski cites Desmond Morris’s famous 1950s studies, which found that non-human primates given pens and paints not only became adept at using them with “a distinct feel for symmetry and balance,” but developed individual styles of drawing. He considers what that indicates:

Art arises from a spiritual longing that all people share: to make our mark on the world and to spend our life energy in a work that rises above the mundane, adding grace to existence. We respond to the light of the world around us by giving expression to our own inner light, and when the two are on the same wavelength, the world seems more brilliant and finely focused.

Insisting that such spiritual longings do not belong to human beings alone, he cites an astonishing case study:

In 1982 Jerome Witkin, a professor of art at Syracuse University and a respected authority on abstract expressionism, was invited to view a collection of drawings by a “mystery artist.” The professor was busy at the time, preparing for a traveling exhibition. Nevertheless, he was sufficiently intrigued to accept the invitation.

“These drawings are very lyrical, very, very beautiful,” the professor said when he saw the portfolio. “They are so positive and affirmative and tense, the energy is so compact and controlled, it’s just incredible.”

“This piece is so graceful, so delicate,” he said of one drawing. “I can’t get most of my students to fill a page like this.”

Only after he had finished his professional evaluation did Witkin learn the identity of the artist: a fourteen-year-old, 8,400-pound Asian elephant named Siri who lived in Syracuse’s Burnet Park Zoo. Siri’s keeper, David Gucwa, had seen her tracing lines with sticks and stones in the dust of her cage. Against the wishes of the zoo’s superintendent, who scoffed at the notion of an artistic elephant, Gucwa had given her pads of paper and charcoal, permitting her to express herself more freely.

When Witkin showed Siri’s drawings to a colleague without context — an expert on children’s drawings charing the university’s art education department — she firmly concluded that they were not done by a child. Witkin himself readily likened them to the work of Willem de Kooning, wishing the painter himself could see Siri’s art.

It was this report of Siri that inspired May Sarton — one of my favorite poets and favorite thinkers — to reimagine these reckonings in a poem. (The footnote of credit in Sarton’s collection is how I discovered Kowalski’s book.)

The drawings were abstract, Delicate, Like Japanese calligraphy. When the painter de Kooning Was shown them, he said, “Interesting. Not done by a child, I think, Or if so, an extraordinary child.” “The artist is an elephant, Sir, Named Siri.”

It had once come about That the keeper noticed Her sensitive trunk Drawing designs in the dust. After an argument With the head of the zoo Who laughed at him, The keeper himself Brought large sheets of paper And boxes of charcoal And laid them at Siri’s feet. For an hour at a time In happy concentration The elephant created designs. Like Japanese calligraphy. What artist’s hand As skillful As that sensuous, sensitive trunk?

Two decades after Iris Murdoch found psychological symmetry between art and morality, locating in both “an occasion for unselfing,” Kowlaski turns to the acts of selflessness and compassion that evince a moral faculty — that fundament of a soul. Pelicans and crows, he notes, have been known to care for blind comrades. Darwin himself reported of a band of monkeys coming to the aid of member seized by an eagle, at the risk of their own lives. But nothing renders such morally tinted actions more vivid and more moving than one nineteenth-century naturalist’s account of a misfire.

Working in an era when “collecting specimens” meant killing creatures, he aimed at a tern but only wounded the bird, which fell helplessly into the sea. Immediately, other terns began circling above “manifesting much apparent solicitude,” until two of them dove down toward their wounded comrade. They lifted him up, one at each wing, carried him several yards, and gently put him down before another two picked him up, and so the group took turns carrying him the entire distance to the shore. The naturalist was so moved by this display of compassion and solidarity that, although he was within shot of the rock on which the wounded tern had been rested, he couldn’t bring himself to finish what he had set out to do.

To witness such a scene is to be stilled with wonder and with humility — which, as Rachel Carson so poignantly wrote, “are wholesome emotions, and they do not exist side by side with a lust for destruction.” A generation after her, and well ahead of our still dawning awakening to the ecological and ethical dignity of other species, Kowalaski reflects:

If we are to keep our family homestead — third stone from the sun — safe for coming generations, we must awaken to a new respect for the family of life.

We are kin to, and must be kind to, all creation. Overcoming speciesism — the illusion of human superiority — will be the next step in our moral and spiritual evolution.

To behold such a display of moral feeling with our own eyes is stirring enough, but to be witnessed back by another creature’s eyes is nothing short of a spiritual experience. In a passage that calls to mind Alan Lightman’s transcendent account of looking into the eyes of an osprey, Kowalski writes:

It is difficult to probe the inward awareness of another being. The realm of what one mystic called “the interior castle” is wholly private and wrapped in solitude. But when we look into another’s eyes — even into the eyes of an animal — we may find a small window into that inner sanctum, a window through which our souls can hail and greet one another.

The act of making eye contact with another being presupposes a conscious self behind either pair of peepers: I see you seeing me, and I am aware that you are aware that we are looking at each other.

Perhaps in the end it is not we who have the power to acknowledge or deny the souls of other creatures but other creatures who confer soul-ness upon us. Kowalski writes:

If by soul we mean our sense of self, our identity as particular persons, then our souls are interwoven with those of other living beings… We know ourselves as human, in part, through our relationships with the nonhuman world.

We are rather unsure of ourselves. What distinguishes our species may be this inward anxiety. While other animals may be endowed with special gifts—acute hearing, keen eyesight, incredible speed — human beings are nothing special. This is both a biological and a moral judgment. Lack of specialization makes us highly adaptable, but it also means we have no fixed form or definite identity. Without many inborn instincts to guide us, we as human beings need models for how to live. We need a sense of our own possibilities and limits, and we find them not only in the artificial rules and restraints imposed by human society but in the lessons for living suggested by biology and the earth itself. We are the younger siblings in life’s family — the perpetual neonates of the animal world. In a fundamental way we need other creatures to tell us who we are.

Out of this arises an urgency more than ethical, more than ecological, but existential — nothing less than examining what we are and why we are here at all:

What profit do we have if we gain the whole world and lose or forfeit our own souls? The human race may survive without the chimpanzees, orangutans, and other wild creatures who share the planet. But we will have attenuated the conditions that are necessary for our own “ensoulment”… And when we look into the mirror there will be less and less to love.

There is a glimmering of eternity about our lives. In the vastness of time and space, our lives are indeed small and ephemeral, yet not utterly insignificant. Our lives do matter. Because we care for one another and have feelings, because we can dream and imagine, because we are the kinds of creatures who make music and create art, we are not merely disconnected fragments of the universe but at some level reflect the beauty and splendor of the whole. And because all life shares in One Spirit, we can recognize this indwelling beauty in other creatures.

Couple The Souls of Animals with John James Audubon — who was both a visionary ahead of his time and, like the tern-shooting naturalist, a product of its blind spots — on other minds and the secret knowledge of animals, then revisit Loren Eiseley on the wonder of being alive lensed through a bouquet of warblers and a reflection on signs vs. omens and our search for meaning lensed through a great blue heron.

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. Is Your Penis Getting Smaller as You Age? This Common Factor Could Hide One to Two Inches.

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

IT PROBABLY SOUNDS like a nightmare scenario to think your penis is getting shorter. Maybe not even being visible at all. But it can happen as you age, and when it does, doctors refer to it as a buried penis.

Now it's not that your penis is physically getting shorter. It's just that most of it is hidden. More on that below.

CONVINCED YOU LOST an inch? Thankfully, your penis isn’t disappearing; it’s just hidden beneath fat tissue.

Justin Dubin, MD, urologist and men’s health specialist at Baptist Health, says that generally when you can’t see the penis, it’s usually because of low abdominal tissue surrounding the penis.

Essentially, your penis is still its regular size, but it doesn’t extend outside the body. Drogo Montague, MD, a urologist in Ohio tells MH what that looks like. “There is an opening where the penis would normally hang, and the head is usually flush with skin, but there’s no shaft outside of the body.”

Now you don’t just wake up one day with inches of your penis vanished. The effect occurs on a continuum, says Dr. Montague. You might notice at first, for instance, that your penis seems to get shorter and shorter. (Though, this is not the same as the small amount of shrinkage that some men see with age, which is due to skin cells around the penis becoming less elastic.)

“This is a serious condition because it will inhibit urination, intimacy, and personal hygiene,” says Scott Miller, MD, urologist and medical director of Wellstar Urology. “It can also strongly impact self-esteem and overall emotional health.”

MOST CASES OF buried penis are due to one thing: obesity.

While the rates of buried penises haven’t been thoroughly studied, Dr. Montague sees more men in his office today dealing with the issue than he has in the past. His booked-up calendar is no coincidence. The World Health Organization reported that 1 in 7 people is living with obesity. And even though we are living in the golden age of GLP-1s, half of adults worldwide are expected to be overweight or obese by 2050.

The penis itself has two erection chambers. About one-third is inside the body and two-thirds are outside in the penile shaft. When you’re overweight or with severe obesity—and noticing a change in length—what’s changing is basically how much of your penis is inside your body and how much is outside.

“With extreme obesity, it’s like the obese body engulfs the penis. A full buried penis is when the entire penis shaft is buried below the surface of the skin,” says Dr. Montague. So it's still there, but you just can't see it all.

There are a few factors, some starting at birth.

There is a low chance of a baby being born with abnormalities in which the ligaments that attach to the penis are weak. Fortunately, Dr. Dubin says this is usually identified and surgically corrected early on.

Another cause can be “any surgery on your penis” that’s gone wrong, says Dr. Dubin. That includes circumcision, a procedure done on 71.2 percent of American guys are circumcised at birth (or even as an adult). If a doctor does not remove an appropriate amount of foreskin, there is a risk of the penis dropping back into the fatty area surrounding it.

But any procedure that involves the penis runs the risk of scar tissue and possible infection. That includes penile injections and penis enlargement.

“The ironic part is that while a lot of these things try to make your penis look bigger or be bigger, the complication is it can make your penis actually smaller and cause buried penis,” says Dr. Dubin.

Lymphedema can cause swelling in the scrotum. As lymph fluid accumulates, you might see the makings of a buried penis.

Also known as acne inversa, the skin condition can create small and extremely painful lumps under the skin. Lumps usually appear in the armpits, inner thighs, and—you guessed it—your groin. This happens because the body mistakenly attacks hair follicles in the sweat glands, causing pockets of pus and other scarring.

Sometimes when the prostate is removed due to prostate cancer surgery, men may lose about an inch of penile length. “That’s the result of pulling the urethra up to attach to the bladder,” says Dr. Montague. Still, it seems like most penile shortening rebounds as time passes after your surgery, so don't let that stop you from getting your prostate checked.

The condition occurs when scar tissue forms in the penis and it causes a curved erection. The curvature may give the appearance of a shorter length. The issue often arises because of injury to the penis during sex or micro-tears that accumulated from sports or physical accidents affecting the genital area. Fortunately, if diagnosed early, there are drugs and procedures that could straighten out the penis. Read more about it here.

WHEN YOU HAVE a buried penis, certain activities become more difficult. Right away, you might find it hard to pee. Dr. Dubin says guys may not be able to get the stream started and might have poor flow. Buried penis can also cause trouble in the form of dribbling and incontinence.

The area is also tough to clean, which leads to a host of issues that might trigger fungal or bacterial infections or skin breakdown. Buried penis is associated, for example, with a rare skin condition called lichen sclerosus. It’s an inflammatory disorder that causes itchy patches. The skin that hosts these patches becomes very delicate.

Beyond that, penetrative sex remains an ongoing issue. “These men can’t have sex or sex is very difficult,” says Dr. Montague.

Mentally, having a buried penis can cause depression and self-esteem issues. “Most men associate their penis with their masculinity, and they associate fertility with masculinity,” says Dr. Dubin. “These kinds of issues can have strong mental health implications.”

IF YOUR BURIED penis is obesity-related, losing weight will definitely help. But keep in mind that, even after weight loss, you might have excess skin and tissue that keeps your penis buried.

“Sometimes, unfortunately, in very obese people, the damage has already been done, and more aggressive treatment options may be required,” Dr. Dubin. In that scenario, you may need surgery—which is also an option for people who don’t lose weight. Dr. Miller says surgeons would focus on removing the surrounding fat and tissue and repositioning the penis.

“That allows the penis to come outside of the body,” says Dr. Montague. “In most buried penis surgeries, skin and fat are cut out.”

Having a buried penis can be embarrassing to talk about, Dr. Dubin says. It's disturbing to have this happen and it can take a toll on your well-being. If you feel it's getting in the way of living fully, consider talking with a counselor or other mental health professional. It's also crucial to see a doctor if you’re having urinary, hygiene, or sexual health issues because of a buried penis.

Cassie Shortsleeve is a Boston-based journalist with more than a decade of experience reporting for some of the nation's largest print and digital publications, including Women's Health, Men's Health, Medscape, Parents, Conde Nast Traveler, and others. She also writes the best-selling Substack newsletter Two Truths and is a co-founder of the non-profit Chamber of Mothers.

Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor, whose app runs several coding agents at once

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Meta Platforms Inc. has acquired artificial intelligence coding startup Conductor in a deal first reported today by Axios. Conductor confirmed it is joining Meta in a post on its website. Terms were not disclosed.

Conductor’s software lets a developer run several coding agents at once, each in an isolated copy of the codebase, and then review and merge what they produce. Supported agents include Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s Cursor, and users pay for them through their own subscriptions and keys. The desktop app runs on Macs. A hosted version, Conductor Cloud, puts agents in sandboxed virtual machines where they can keep working for hours, and users can check on them from an iPhone app.

Engineers at Meta were using Conductor well before the deal. When the startup announced its Series A in March, it named Meta, Google LLC and Spotify Technology SA among the companies with dozens of engineers on the product. Conductor now says on its website that more than 100,000 people use it.

People familiar with the deal told Axios that Meta expects the Conductor team’s speed at shipping products to help it build its next generation of AI coding tools. The acquisition follows two Meta model releases last month that both pitched coding as a strength. On Oct. 15, Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open-weights version of its Muse Spark model aimed at coding and long-running agent work. Meta’s more capable Muse Wonder models stay closed inside its own Muse Code terminal and application programming interface.

The Conductor deal landed the same day OpenAI said it plans to acquire developer tools startup Pierre Computer. OpenAI had already announced plans in June to buy Ona, which runs coding agents in cloud sandboxes.

Local copies of the Mac app keep working until early 2027, when the team expects to release a new interface it has not yet described. New models and critical bug fixes stop arriving at that point, and Conductor will delete the app’s user data. The company said it has never sold Conductor user data or trained models on it, and does not plan to.

Chief Executive Charlie Holtz and Chief Technology Officer Jackson de Campos founded the company, formally Melty Inc., in 2024. Conductor raised a $22 million Series A in March from Spark Capital and Matrix. Y Combinator and the founders of Notion and Linear are also backers.

This Genius Trick Makes Perfectly Portioned Cinnamon Rolls—No Ruler or Guessing Required

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

This clever little move turns your knife into a measuring guide for cinnamon rolls.

I have no objection to a shortcut in the kitchen. I’m happy to let boxed cake mix handle dessert or a great jar of pasta sauce get dinner moving. But I just can’t make peace with cinnamon rolls from a can. I want to love them. I appreciate the convenience, and I understand the appeal of having warm cinnamon rolls before the coffee is finished brewing. They just never quite satisfy that craving for a warm, deliciously gooey cinnamon roll.

Some viral upgrades make a compelling case—particularly the heavy cream bath and generous additions of butter and brown sugar. But my long-standing love for cinnamon rolls has much more to do with the soft, pillowy dough, so I’m willing to wait through a rise or two.

Having committed to that, though, I’m still interested in anything that makes the process easier. So when I saw a video of someone flipping a knife over a log of cinnamon roll dough to mark perfectly even portions, I wanted to try it. Cutting equal slices by eye can involve a surprising amount of second-guessing when you’d really just like to get them in the pan. I made our classic cinnamon roll recipe and put the trick to the test.

The clever part of this trick is that the knife becomes its own measurement. Rather than judging the thickness of each slice, you use the width of the blade to mark equal portions along the dough roll before slicing it into pieces.

Once your dough is filled and rolled into a log, gently lay the blade flat across the top at one end, with the knife running crosswise over the log. Then flip it onto its opposite flat side, moving along the dough one blade-width at a time. It looks a little like the knife is doing small somersaults, with its edge leaving a light indentation at each turn.

Continue down the log, using just enough pressure to leave visible marks. Then go back and slice through the dough at those marks.

This worked beautifully with our classic cinnamon rolls, but the same technique would work with just about any cinnamon roll recipe. The turning motion was simple, and the knife left an evenly spaced cutting guide along the dough. Once the marks were there, I could slice the rolls without measuring each one or estimating where the next cut should go.

I particularly liked being able to see all the portions before I started cutting. It made the job feel settled: The spacing was already worked out, and all I had to do was follow it. For something that takes so little effort, it’s a useful bit of precision.

This is the kind of cinnamon roll shortcut I can get behind. I still get the homemade rolls I wanted, but there’s one less thing to fuss over before the pan goes into the oven.

Crypto PACs eye 2028 “new map” as Democrats take Congress

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Crypto super PACs spent more than $176 million on the midterms, but the Democratic sweep raises the prospect of tougher industry scrutiny.

Two years after crypto money helped drive Sherrod Brown out of the Senate, roughly $64 million couldn’t keep him from returning.

Brown’s victory over Republican Jon Husted in Ohio delivered the industry its biggest electoral loss of the 2026 midterms as Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. The sweep also puts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, one of crypto’s fiercest critics, in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee.

Crypto super PACs spent about $176 million across 100 seats during the election cycle, including primaries, according to Reuters, up from more than $130 million in 2024. Fairshake and its affiliated PACs accounted for $154.5 million across 89 races.

“The next Congress will bring a fundamentally different environment for crypto in Washington, and the industry should expect significantly more scrutiny,” Kyle Bligen, executive director at the Decentralization Research Center, told Cointelegraph.

Fairshake, meanwhile, is left with more than $67 million heading to the 2028 elections. “Newly elected and current members will have a choice: protect consumers and American jobs or fight progress,” spokesperson Geoff Vetter told Cointelegraph in an email. “We will be watching and ‘28 is a new map.”

Ohio was the industry’s biggest bet as crypto PACs put more than $64 million into keeping Senator Jon Husted in office. His opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, won the special election to complete former Sen. JD Vance’s term, which ends in January 2029. He could seek a senior role on the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

Brown’s comeback came two years after crypto’s biggest win in 2024, when Fairshake spent $40 million to help Bernie Moreno unseat him in Ohio’s other Senate seat. Some industry leaders treated that result as a warning to Congress. Gemini exchange co-founder Cameron Winklevoss declared on X: “This is what happens when you mess with the crypto army”.

This year, crypto spending was part of a much larger flood of outside money. Independent expenditures in the race topped $350 million, while Brown turned the crypto spending into a campaign theme, writing “I’ll be damned if crypto billionaires decide this race,” in a campaign message.

The loss in Ohio may weaken the perception that defying crypto PACs carries an electoral cost in Washington. Before the vote, a Republican crypto lobbyist told Politico that a Brown win would “neuter Fairshake’s perceived Sword of Damocles.”

Nebraska, meanwhile, offered crypto PACs a significant win, with Sen. Pete Ricketts retaining his seat after Fairshake affiliate Defend American Jobs spent $13.5 million opposing independent challenger Dan Osborn.

“As the biggest spender in the Nebraska Senate race, we’re proud to have helped Sen. Ricketts weather the waves of a hard-fought cycle,” wrote Vetter. “Fairshake played a meaningful role in winning competitive races across the country in 2026 and we will do it again in 2028.” The PAC’s other Senate wins came in Republican strongholds, including Barry Moore in Alabama and Andy Barr in Kentucky.

Other spending failed to deliver the intended results, both in primaries and in November. The Fairshake network’s roughly $10 million spent opposing Juliana Stratton in the Illinois Democratic primary failed to block her nomination. She later won the Senate seat. In Massachusetts, John Deaton lost despite roughly $700,000 in spending by crypto-backed Commonwealth Unity Fund to help elect him. Ken Paxton, who received crypto PAC backing in his successful Texas Republican runoff against John Cornyn, went on to lose to James Talarico.

The House brought another setback when digital assets subcommittee chair Bryan Steil lost to Democrat Mitchell Berman despite $1.9 million in crypto PAC funding.

The shift in congressional control could slow crypto legislation, but BitGo CEO and co-founder Mike Belshe said the election results would not alter the industry’s trajectory. “Crypto has continued to move forward under different administrations and different political majorities. The GENIUS Act is now law, stablecoin rules are moving ahead, and regulators are continuing to work on tokenization and digital asset markets.”Democratic victories could also bring crypto supporters into the Senate. Advocacy group Stand With Crypto counted 19 winning Senate candidates it classified as pro-crypto and eight as anti-crypto, with 33 of the 35 Senate races called as of 9:45 p.m. UTC on Nov. 4.

Despite the crypto PAC spending against him in Texas, Talarico voted for the Texas Bitcoin reserve as a state lawmaker and is rated by the group as strongly supportive of crypto.

For industry advocates, the next challenge is building relationships with incoming lawmakers. Jessica Martinez, US policy director at Fireblocks, told Cointelegraph that many newly elected members had limited records on crypto, making “educating members early” key to shaping the Democratic policy agenda.

ChatGPT Is Getting a GIF Maker Powered by OpenAI's Unannounced Images 2.6 Model

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

ChatGPT Is Getting a GIF Maker Powered by OpenAI's Unannounced Images 2.6 Model

The internet may soon have an unlimited supply of AI-generated dancing cats, courtesy of ChatGPT.

OpenAI is rolling out a feature that lets users generate animated GIFs directly inside ChatGPT, according to The Verge. The feature reportedly comes powered by its new image-generation model called Images 2.6, which OpenAI has yet to formally introduce through its usual product announcements.

Users can describe an animation in plain English or upload an existing photo and ask ChatGPT to bring it to life. Once the GIF is generated, they can adjust its playback speed, inspect individual frames, make edits, and share the finished animation.

OpenAI demonstrated the capability with a simple request: “can you make a gif of a cat dancing?” The resulting interface reportedly includes controls to change animation speed and examine the GIF frame by frame.

We tried generating GIFs using ChatGPT, but the feature was not available on our accounts at the time of testing. In our interaction, the model generates a series of frames, but not the animation.

The rollout appears to be gradual, so users may have to keep asking for their dancing cats a little longer.

The GIF maker is reportedly part of a broader Images 2.6 update that promises faster image generation. The Verge reports that OpenAI is bringing the model to ChatGPT and Codex users across web, desktop, and mobile platforms.

Developers are also getting two new API models, GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst, designed for faster generation and higher-quality results, respectively. OpenAI has not yet published a standalone announcement detailing the new model's capabilities, and we could not independently test its performance.

The update follows the September release of ChatGPT Images 2.5, which introduced sharper details, more precise editing, and generation speeds up to 50% faster than its predecessor.

In our previous testing, Images 2.5 went head-to-head with Google's Nano Banana 2 across six categories, with each model winning three. OpenAI's model delivered particularly impressive illustration quality and improved on the oversharpening problems that affected earlier versions, although it still made mistakes when rendering text.

The move into GIF generation also comes months after OpenAI shut down Sora, its standalone AI video-generation app, in March. Animated GIFs are considerably simpler than the videos Sora generated, but the new feature brings a form of motion generation directly into ChatGPT without requiring a separate application.

OpenAI has not provided a specific date for when every ChatGPT account will receive GIF generation.

North Carolina Passes New Limits on Property Tax Levies

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

On Tuesday, North Carolina voters narrowly approved House Bill 1089, which proposed a limit on property tax increases. The amendment needed 60% of voters to support it in order to pass. It received 60.4% support.

The amendment does not specify the terms of those limits. Instead, that will be up to the North Carolina General Assembly to decide.

Proponents, including North Caroline House Speaker Destin Hall, contended that surging property assessments have enabled local governments to impose excessive tax burdens on residents without delivering proportional public services. Last year, Hall formed the House Select Committee on Property Tax Reduction and Reform, a 23-member committee to examine property taxes in the state.

“Families are getting ripped off as some, but by no means all, local governments rake in billions more than inflation and population growth warrant,” Hall said in a press release earlier this year.

Support for the amendment fell across party lines. Conservatives and commercial organizations supported the measure, arguing that the amendment would help curb local government spending and protect property owners.

Political pundits theorized that the ballot measures were meant to entice Republican voters to the polls during an off-election year. But Western Carolina University Professor Chris Cooper told NPR's All Things Considered the theory didn't hold much weight to him.

"The notion that North Carolinians were not going to show up and vote from the Republican persuasion, but now they are because of a constitutional amendment, is on there, frankly that stretches credibility for me a little bit."

But critics of the proposal said that creating a property tax cap would hobble local governments. Further, the North Carolina Housing Coalition argued that the proposal would most benefit larger corporate property owners while providing little benefit to owners of single-family homes.

Tamika Walker Kelly, president of the North Carolina Association of Educators, criticized the bill for favoring “tax breaks over classrooms.”

“When local revenue is constrained, schools feel it immediately with overcrowded classrooms, aging school buildings and educators stretched too thin,” Walker Kelly told NC Newsline. “A constitutional cap does not protect struggling families, it protects the largest landowners in the state, while the families who depend on public schools are left with less.”

In the U.S., property tax rates are determined at the local level and vary widely. The average effective property tax rate on owner-occupied housing in North Carolina is .66%, which is relatively low compared with states like New Jersey and Illinois, where the effective tax rate is 1.88%, according to Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax policy nonprofit.

GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:

According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

Crypto Market Today, Nov. 4: Bitcoin Stages Sharp Recovery as Wall Street Rallies and Regulatory Hopes Return

📅 Nov 04, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Bitcoin reclaimed $80,000 as cryptocurrencies rallied alongside Wall Street following the midterm elections, with Ethereum leading gains among major digital assets.

As of early evening on Nov. 4, Bitcoin (BTC +3.35%) rose 3.64% to $80,156.15, Ethereum (ETH +5.44%) rose 6.58% to $2,421.50, and Solana (SOL +1.42%) rose 2.19% to $94.94.

Cryptocurrency markets staged a broad recovery on Wednesday as the conclusion of the U.S. midterm elections helped ease political uncertainty that had weighed on risk assets in recent weeks. Bitcoin, which had fallen as low as $75,700 amid sustained selling pressure, rebounded above $80,000, while Ethereum led gains among major cryptocurrencies, climbing more than 6% to a two-week high above $2,400.

The recovery coincided with a broader rally across U.S. equities, as investors responded positively to the election results and the prospect of greater policy stability. Declining oil prices and easing Treasury yields provided additional support for risk appetite, helping lift cryptocurrencies alongside traditional financial markets.

Among key crypto funds, iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT +2.91%) rose 2.91%, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC +2.84%) rose 2.87%, and iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA +5.72%) rose 5.72%.

The rebound follows an extended period of weakness that resulted in more than $1 billion of outflows from spot Bitcoin ETFs. Whether Wednesday's gains mark the beginning of a sustained recovery will likely depend on improving ETF flows.

In the wake of the Democratic sweep of Congress, crypto investors should be watching for a potential shift in the regulatory landscape. Democratic lawmakers are reportedly considering revisions to the stalled CLARITY Act that could expand the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) authority, strengthen investor protections, and impose additional restrictions on government officials' cryptocurrency activities. Although discussions remain preliminary, renewed legislative momentum could help resolve regulatory uncertainty that has weighed on the industry for months and establish a clearer framework heading into 2027.

In the near term, investors will be looking for confirmation that Wednesday's rebound has staying power. Bitcoin holding above the psychologically important $80,000 level and reclaiming $82,000 would be encouraging signs of renewed buying momentum.

Ultimately, the combination of regulatory developments and reclamation of key levels could provide a foundation for a more sustained recovery. However, macroeconomic uncertainty, shifting interest rate expectations, and lingering weakness across the broader cryptocurrency market suggest investors should remain prepared for continued volatility.
